gendto.komentar.berkas:
PRIVATE mirror of the payload types in {gen}, plus two-way converters.

Deliberately without json tags: the structs here are never serialised. What goes on the
wire stays the generated type ({alias}.*), whose shape the contract decides. This mirror is
used INSIDE the package only — so when a generated type name shifts, the only file that has
to be regenerated is this one, not every handler.

What is NOT mirrored, and that is on purpose:
  - *RequestObject/*ResponseObject/*JSONResponse types — those are the strict-server seam,
    a handler must return the original generated type;
  - the shared envelope — it is single, in the shared generated package;
  - oneOf union types — they carry their own methods over json.RawMessage.
gendto.komentar.dtoconv:
The mapping helpers ({pkgKonv}.Slice/Ptr/Map) live in {jalurKonv} — ONE copy for the whole
repository, not one copy per feature package. A single feature may use more than one
generated package, so these helpers must not be pinned to a feature package.
gendto.komentar.uji:
Converter round trip: proof that the mapping loses nothing. Compilation only proves the
types line up — not that every field is mapped. This test fills the wire value with
non-zero values down to the leaves, spins it wire -> mirror -> wire, and demands DeepEqual.
A field that was forgotten shows up as a zero value on the result side and this test fails.

kontrak.komentar.wiring_berkas:
Contract tag: {tag} (package {pkg})
Operations: {operasi} — {dijaga} guarded, {publik} public.

This file holds only DATA derived from the contract plus one thin mounting function. Every
authorisation decision lives in the platform package — do not copy that logic here.
kontrak.komentar.spec_by_operation:
SpecByOperation maps a contract operationId to its guard category ({aturan}).

Operations with `security: []` are DELIBERATELY absent here: they have no guard category, and
that is what the public-operations list is for. Adding them would write a "no permissions but not
auth-only" entry — a shape the permission checker treats as a BROKEN map. Such an entry is never
read today, but it is a trap waiting for the next reader.
kontrak.komentar.spec_by_route:
SpecByRoute maps "METHOD /pattern" to a guard category, for the GROUP-level middleware that runs
BEFORE the generated layer binds parameters or the body. It holds only operations mounted into
the protected group; public operations are not guarded.
kontrak.komentar.public_routes:
PublicRoutes holds the "METHOD /pattern" of this tag's `security: []` operations — routes that
ARE mounted but are DELIBERATELY absent from SpecByRoute because they are not guarded.

It exists for tests, and for a narrow reason: the test helper demands a TWO-WAY match between
mounted routes and spec keys, so without this list every module with a public operation fails in
both directions at once. Before this list was generated, the only alternative was rewriting it BY
HAND in each module's test: a second copy of the contract, ungated, that would drift silently.

It is NOT a guard map and must not be used as one — the routes here are precisely the ones with
no guard category at all.
kontrak.komentar.v2_paths:
V2Paths holds the route patterns whose failures must use the single envelope even when they
originate in group-level middleware — before the request has touched feature code at all.
kontrak.komentar.public_ops: publicOps holds this tag's operations that the contract declares as `security: []`.
kontrak.komentar.guard_by_operation:
guardByOperation is the guard layer that knows the operationId from the generated layer ITSELF
rather than from route matching — so it still fails closed even if the per-route map is wrong.

The generated handler passes the server language's METHOD name (PascalCase), not the contract
operationId (camelCase); the map stays keyed by the CONTRACT operationId.
kontrak.komentar.content_by_operation:
contentByOperation is the FIRST element of the middleware slice — but because the generated
handler wraps middleware ITERATIVELY (the LAST element becomes the OUTERMOST wrapper and runs
FIRST), being "first in the slice" actually means it executes AFTER the permission check: auth
and permissions first, body content afterwards. Do not reorder the slice without understanding
this — reordered, the body is validated BEFORE the session and permissions are checked.

The manifest is derived straight from the contract's requestBody. Operations without a manifest
entry return the handler unwrapped — zero body reads for operations that do not need one.
kontrak.komentar.mount:
Mount mounts every operation of this tag. The implementor supplies only the implementation; the
permission map, the guard chain, the error hooks, and the envelope path list all come from the
contract.

Each operation is mounted into the group its contract calls for — public into the public group
with no session guard, the rest into the protected group behind the guard. Because Mount decides,
double registration and accidentally-open operations are both inexpressible.
kontrak.komentar.shared_berkas:
The shared schemas are defined ONCE in the shared generated package; this file only wires the
names that the generated server file references over to that definition.

These are ALIASES (`=`), so the type is the SAME across packages — not merely a similar shape.
Written without `=`, each package gets its own type again and the whole point is lost.
kontrak.komentar.content_berkas:
Per-operation requestBody constraint manifest for tag {tag} (package {pkg}). Consumed by the
content-validation layer in the wiring file.

Operations without a JSON object requestBody (GET/DELETE, array-at-the-root bodies) have NO entry
here — that is DELIBERATE, not forgotten coverage.
kontrak.komentar.permission_tipe:
Permission is a permission name recognised by the contract catalogue ({aturan}). This type stops
the permission checker from accepting free-form strings — a name absent from the catalogue fails
to compile rather than failing silently at runtime.
kontrak.komentar.permission_semua: AllPermissions holds the whole catalogue; used by gates and tests.
kontrak.komentar.permission_parse: ParsePermission turns a string into a Permission if the catalogue contains it.
kontrak.komentar.error_code_tipe:
ErrorCode is an error code recognised by the contract catalogue ({aturan}).

Be careful reading this as "the compiler guards it": UNTYPED constants are still accepted here —
only typed string VARIABLES are rejected. What actually closes the catalogue is the gate that
parses source, not this type.
kontrak.komentar.error_code_semua: AllErrorCodes holds the whole catalogue; used by gates and tests.
kontrak.komentar.error_code_parse: ParseErrorCode turns a string into an ErrorCode if the catalogue contains it.
kontrak.komentar.shared_spec_deskripsi: Derived document — DO NOT EDIT. Generated from the contract's envelope file and its bundle.
kontrak.komentar.katalog_permission:
Permission catalogue — a CLOSED vocabulary ({aturan}).

Source of truth for the vocabulary: the seed data (the permission table's rows).

Adding a new permission = three steps, in this order:
  1. add it to the seed data (without this no role can hold it)
  2. add it to the `permissions` list below
  3. use it in the `x-permission` of the operation it guards

NEW entries must follow the <DOMAIN>_<ACTION> pattern. The names under `legacyNames` violate that
pattern and are DELIBERATELY left alone — renaming them means a data migration on rows already
referenced by roles in production. Do NOT copy their style.

genmodule.komentar.header:
Regen: standard gen module --tag {tag} --pkg {pkg} --apply

This file may still be rewritten. Once the module is hand-wired, freeze it: its name changes
from {gen} to {beku} and the generator stops touching it (B-03).
genmodule.komentar.register:
Register mounts all {jumlah} operation(s) of tag `{tag}` through the generated router.

All permission wiring comes from the contract via {alias}.Mount: the permission map, the guard
chain, the error hook, and the path list. An implementor only supplies an impl of
{alias}.StrictServerInterface — see the handler file.

What Mount does NOT guarantee: the tenant boundary. That lives in the query predicate and cannot
be derived from the contract (T-01) — it is born in the hand-written query layer.

# store is still nil, and that is deliberate

The query layer has not been written, so there is nothing to fill the store with. This module
compiles and boots, but every one of its operations PANICS the moment it is called. That is a
LOUD failure — the alternative (a fake store returning empty results) would make a module that
does not work yet look healthy, and that is a far more expensive class of bug.

What to do once the query layer exists: replace the `nil` below with your store constructor, then
freeze the module.

# If this module needs dependencies beyond the database handle

The shape below is the PLAIN shape, and it is the only one the generator can know. A module that
needs more (a cache, an object-store client, signing keys, other services) uses the CURRIED
shape — Register returns a function, and the application entry point calls it with the
dependencies:

	func Register(dep *Dep) func(public, protected *{router}, db *{db}) {
		return func(_, protected *{router}, db *{db}) {
			{alias}.Mount(nil, protected, &handler{svc: newService(newStore(db), dep)})
		}
	}

That need is NOT in the contract, so the generator cannot see it — and that is one of the two
reasons a hand-wired module must never be regenerated (the second: extra steps in the service
layer). If you switch to the curried shape, its caller at the application entry point changes
too.
genmodule.komentar.handler:
handler holds the service and implements the generated strict server.

It is the ONLY layer that names generated types (B-01). It has exactly two jobs: unpack the
RequestObject into internally-typed arguments, and wrap the internal result into the generated
response. Zero raw response writes (B-02) — the response is written by the generated layer from
the returned value, and errors travel up as errors to be mapped by the central middleware through
the hook in Mount.
genmodule.komentar.handler_ctx:
The tenant context is read through {ctx}.From(ctx) — ONE lookup from the context.Context the
strict server hands over, without first type-asserting to the HTTP framework's own context type.
That assert only works because the generator happens to pass the original context straight
through, and no document promises it.

If this module later needs the real framework context (raw body, headers, multipart), add your
own accessor AFTER freezing — not in this skeleton, because most operations do not need it and an
unused import is a compile error.
genmodule.komentar.service:
service is where the rules that are neither wire shape nor query live: guards based on the
request context, injection of non-database dependencies (notifiers, file stores, clocks), and the
ordering of calls across stores.

This generated skeleton is still pure delegation — each method forwards as-is to the store. That
is an honest STARTING state, not the final shape: as soon as an operation needs more than one
store call, or a dependency other than the database handle, this is where it gets written.

And that is also why a hand-wired module must never be regenerated: the generator cannot see the
dependencies you injected into this struct.
genmodule.komentar.service_new:
newService builds a service over the given store.

It accepts nil: until the query layer exists, Register injects nil — see the register file.
genmodule.komentar.store:
store is the complete set of database operations this module needs, one method per contract
operation.

All of them use INTERNAL types (the `dto*` mirrors from the DTO mirror file), not generated
types. That is what frees the implementor from the wire shape, and it is what B-01 demands: when
a generated type name shifts, the only things that need regenerating are the mirror and the
handler, not every query.

`ctx *{ctx}` is on EVERY method, including the ones that only take a bare id. That is not
decoration: without ctx the implementor has no way to attach a tenant predicate, and a raw id
from the path goes straight to the database — a permission holder in tenant A could read, modify,
and delete tenant B's rows just by knowing the id. T-02 demands the SIGNATURE be fixed, not a
post-load check be added: a caller that fails to pass the context must FAIL TO COMPILE.
genmodule.tenancy.checklist:
# Cross-tenant checklist — feature `{fitur}` (tag `{tag}`)

Generated by genmodule from the contract. It is NOT code: your concrete store type, your tenant
context constructor, your database driver, and your assertion library are four APIs this standard
does not declare — and a generator that invented them would emit a test that compiles nowhere
except in one project. What is portable is the obligation, and that is what this file holds.

COPY it into a real test next to the query layer, then DELETE this file.

## Why the query layer is not generated

The tenant boundary lives in the query predicate and cannot be derived from the contract (T-01).
A generator that touches that layer is a generator that invents a security boundary. Until you
write it, this module boots with a nil store and every operation stops hard when called.

## Methods that MUST have a tenant-predicate test

Only methods shaped `(ctx)` and `(ctx, id string)` are listed here, and that is a deliberate
limit: methods that carry a payload write rows when run, so running them without a fixture is not
something that generalises. The `(ctx, id)` shape is in fact the class that LEAKS MOST OFTEN — a
bare id from the path, straight to the database, with no tenant predicate (T-02).

{metode}

## Two assertions per method, and both are required

1. **The tenant predicate IS in the emitted SQL.** Assert the SQL, not the call shape: a test
   built on a fake store never touches SQL, and therefore cannot catch this class of defect at
   all. Fill in the predicate that is CORRECT for your model — a direct tenant column, one
   reached through a relation, or a territory coverage filter. The generator does not know which,
   and guessing produces a test that is green for the wrong predicate.
2. **A context WITHOUT a tenant touches the database not at all.** Not "returns an error": a
   correct error response on top of a query with no tenant boundary is still a leak (T-03). What
   is asserted is that ZERO queries were emitted.

To capture SQL without a real database, use your data layer's dry-run mode if it has one — a
deliberately unreachable DSN is enough, because the SQL is built without being executed.

## Methods whose table really is GLOBAL

Remove them from this list, and write the reason in the tenant-scope architecture test — not
here, and not only in a commit message. A silent exception is the new silent pass.

## Evidence that does NOT count for ticking this list

That a permission checker is present, that CI is green, that the guard-category gate passes, or
that the UI never offers such an id (T-04). This class of hole is only visible through ids the UI
never offered.

cli.bantuan_gen:
standard gen <kind> [options]

  kind: {dikenal}

  common                              permission catalog, error-code catalog, shared schema document
  wiring  --tag <TAG> --pkg <PKG>     route wiring + content manifest for one tag
  dto     [--only <FEATURE>]          private dto mirrors per feature
  module  --tag <TAG> --pkg <PKG>     feature module skeleton (register/handler/service/repository)
          [--feature <DIR>] [--out <DIR>] [--force]

  --apply  actually write. WITHOUT it everything is a dry run: the plan is reported, exit 0,
           and not a single file is touched.
  --force  overwrite a module that has been FROZEN. Freezing means its files were hand-married;
           anything added there is lost without a compile error.
cli.bantuan_freeze:
standard freeze --pkg <PKG> [--feature <DIR>] [--apply]

  End a module's regeneration period: skeleton files carrying the generated suffix are renamed to
  ordinary files, and from then on the generator REFUSES to touch that module.

  Before freezing, work through the cross-tenant checklist the generator wrote in the module
  directory and DELETE the file — gate:tenancy-checklist reds any frozen module still carrying it.

  --apply  actually rename. Without it: report only, exit 0.
cli.bantuan_gate:
standard gate [--lapis <LAYER>] [--only <STEP>]

  steps (and the gate names each plays):
  {langkah}

  layers: {lapis}

  With no flags: every step, in order, stopping at the FIRST red one.
  Exit code 1 = violations found; 2 = the tool failed, so the check did NOT run.
  A selection that leaves no step at all is REJECTED, not treated as passing.
gen.menjalankan_skrip: running {alat} with working directory {cwd} — contract scripts read the config from their working directory, not from a flag.
cli.bantuan_verify:
standard verify [--update-golden]

  Self-test for this package — not a check on your project. It ignores the working directory
  and always works on package files: rules/, the message catalogs, and the fixture project
  under tooling/testdata/.

  Six stages, ALL of them run — a complete report is more useful than stopping at stage one:

  1  rules-lint over rules/ and the three document entry points
  2  message catalog parity id vs en: keys AND the variable names within each key
  3  doctor over the fixture project
  4  the fixture pipeline (gen common -> wiring -> module -> dto) into a temporary directory,
     every file compared against tooling/testdata/golden/
  5  a BILINGUAL run: the same pipeline plus every gate, re-run with language en, then its
     output scanned for Indonesian words smuggled in as variable VALUES
  6  an origin-project-name scan over the WHOLE folder (process documents aside), plus the
     INSTALL.md inventories checked both ways against reality: third-party modules nailed into
     the tool sources, the four platform package contracts, and the template placeholder list

  --update-golden  REWRITES the golden files instead of comparing them. Use it deliberately when
                   the generators really did change; the diff is what gets reviewed. WITHOUT this
                   flag verify writes no file at all outside its temporary directories.

  Exit codes: 0 pass. 1 = the check ran and found violations.
  2 = the tool itself failed, so the check did NOT run.
verify.ringkas_ok: verify is green: {tahap} stage(s) ran, {berkas} golden file(s) matched.
verify.ringkas_temuan: verify: {jumlah} finding(s) across {tahap} stage(s) that ran.
verify.alat_gagal: stage "{nama}": the TOOL itself failed, so its check did NOT run — {sebab}
verify.pesan_kunci_hilang: message catalog: key "{kunci}" exists in {ada} but is missing from {hilang}.
verify.pesan_var_beda: message catalog: key "{kunci}" uses different variable names per language — id: {id}; en: {en}.
verify.fixture_tak_ditulis: {alat} did not write {berkas}. A step that is silently skipped produces exactly zero diff, just like a step that did its job — so a missing file is reported, not treated as a match.
verify.golden_hilang: golden {berkas} does not exist. Run `standard verify --update-golden`, then review the diff before committing.
verify.golden_basi: golden {berkas} has no counterpart in the fixture pipeline output — delete the file, or refresh it with --update-golden.
verify.golden_diperbarui: golden refreshed: {ditulis} file(s) written, {dihapus} deleted, in {dir}.
verify.dwibahasa_kata: language {bahasa} run: the Indonesian word "{kata}" shows up in tool output — {baris}
verify.dwibahasa_seragam: language {bahasa} run: {berkas} is identical to the golden version. Prose the generator writes into the code it emits must come from the catalog; a file that does not change when the language changes has its prose nailed into the code.
verify.dwibahasa_golden_hilang: language {bahasa} run: there is no golden for {berkas}, so the bilingual comparison for that file did NOT run.
verify.probe_tidak_merah: red probe {nama} exited 0 — its sabotage did NOT land, so the {bahasa} failure sentence was never rendered and nothing was scanned.
verify.asal_temuan: the origin project name appears in {berkas}:{baris} — {teks}
verify.asal_pengecualian_mati: scanner exemption "{nama}" was never used even once over this package. Every exemption is a path where the scan does NOT run; one that is never used points at the wrong place, or is left over from a folder structure that has since changed.
verify.install_hilang: {berkas} does not exist, so the prerequisite inventory, the platform package contract, and the placeholder list cannot be checked against anything.
verify.install_blok_hilang: INSTALL.md has no inventory block "{blok}". A missing block shrinks its check to zero without producing a single finding.
verify.install_blok_terbuka: inventory block "{blok}" in INSTALL.md is opened but never closed. Everything that follows is read as part of that block.
verify.install_tak_dikenali: INSTALL.md block "{blok}" line {baris}: its shape was not recognised, so it is NOT compared against the scan — reported, not dropped: {teks}
verify.prasyarat_tak_terdaftar: third-party module {entri} is nailed into the tool sources ({situs}) but is not listed in INSTALL.md block "{blok}". A portability assumption has to be READABLE, not inferred from a green gate.
verify.prasyarat_basi: INSTALL.md block "{blok}" lists {entri}, but no site in the tool sources nails it down any more. A stale declaration lies to the reader who trusts it most.
verify.simbol_tak_terdaftar: platform package symbol {entri} is emitted by the generators ({situs}) but is absent from INSTALL.md block "{blok}". A consumer who does not provide it gets generated code that will not compile.
verify.simbol_basi: INSTALL.md block "{blok}" names symbol {entri}, but no generator emits it any more.
verify.placeholder_tak_terdaftar: placeholder {{{entri}}} is used by a template this package ships but is not listed in INSTALL.md block "{blok}". A placeholder nobody knows to fill gets left behind, and one left behind inside paths: keeps its workflow from ever firing.
verify.placeholder_basi: INSTALL.md block "{blok}" lists placeholder {{{entri}}}, but no template uses it.
verify.install_tanpa_keterangan: INSTALL.md block "{blok}": entry {entri} has no description column. The entry name alone does not tell the reader what they must do — for the platform package contract, that column is what carries the symbol's OBLIGATION.
